title: Abdul El-Sayed’s Michigan primary victory is the latest win for progressives challenging establishment-backed Democrats – live
summary: The former public health official’s victory in Michigan US Senate primary race comes after progressive wins in New York and Colorado
body: In a speech laced with anti-Muslim animus, Donald Trump just accused Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for the US Senate from Michigan, who is Muslim, of being motivated by deep-seated antisemitism. El-Sayed, who narrowly won the Democratic primary in Michigan despite $30m in negative ads paid for by groups linked to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), has campaigned with Jewish supporters, but strongly condemned Israel’s killing and mistreatment of Palestinians. According to Trump, El-Sayed is “a hater of Jews and a hater of Israel”. “Just say this guy hates Jews. Somebody said, ‘Oh, that’s a little strong.’ No, he hates Jews and he hates Israel,” Trump said. “He’s a man of hate.” The president then mockingly pronounced El-Sayed’s name, clearly stressing its Arabic origins, eliciting boos from his supporters in Nevada, just as his earlier reference to “Barack Hussein Obama” had. At another point in the speech, Trump also made a sarcastic reference to “the lovely Islamic Republic of Iran”. Earlier on Wednesday, as other Republicans released frankly racist statements attempting to cast El-Sayed as a Muslim extremist, El-Sayed addressed Jewish Americans in comments carried live by Fox News. “To my Jewish American sisters and brothers, one of the most indelible memories of this campaign will have been the opportunity to break bread with you at seder,” El-Sayed said, “and listening to sisters and brothers who said, ‘I want to join this movement because Aipac doesn’t speak for me; because I understand that self-determination for one people does not require the quenching of self-determination for another people; that unless all of us are free, none of us are free,’ I want to tell you the great gift that you’ve given me.” “I want you to know,” he continued, “that my commitment to your safety, my commitment to Jewish safety, is the same commitment that I have to the safety of my own daughters.” Apparently referring to these comments, which were carried live on the president’s favorite network, Trump said: “Now he’s going around saying, ‘No, I love everybody … ’ He doesn’t love everybody. Put him in office, you’re going to find out what he loves. He doesn’t love Israel. He doesn’t love Jewish people. He hates them. He hates them with a passion that burns in his heart and is not a fricking thing he can do about it. There’s not a thing he can do about it ’cause he hates them.” The idea that many non-Jews hold a deep-seated, unreasoning, anti-Jewish animus is a frequent claim made by Israeli politicians, including Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. “When I watch Abdul,” Trump said later in the speech, “he’s full of shit.” Donald Trump is now speaking to supporters in Nevada, and so far he is giving a standard campaign rally speech, running through his standard boasts about how well he is doing and repeating false claims he has made again and again. The president began by claiming that he had won Nevada in the 2024 election “in a landslide”. In fact, he won the state by 46,008 votes over Kamala Harris. Four years earlier, Trump had lost the state to Joe Biden by a similar if slightly smaller margin of 33,596 votes. In a speech that was billed as a presidential address on the economy, but is in effect a midterm campaign rally for Republican candidates that support him, Trump went on to repeat a series of false claims, including: his wildly inflated estimate that $19tn has been invested by foreign businesses since he returned to office; “the economy is the greatest economy we’ve ever had by far”; the fiction that “25 million poured through our southern border” during the Biden administration. Trump also told his entirely invented tale that “the king of Saudi Arabia” told him last year: “a year ago your country was dead; it was a dead country. We never thought it was coming back. And now you have the hottest country anywhere in the world.” In fact, during his visit to Riyadh in 2025, Trump told the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, the US was “the hottest country in the world”, a claim that he previously made at least a dozen times in public comments during his first term, starting with rally speeches ahead of the 2018 midterms, and has repeated dozens of times since. Lawyers for Donald Trump asked a federal judge in Miami on Wednesday to pause an earlier order that requires financial information for 400 of his business entities to be disclosed to the BBC, as the British broadcaster works to defend itself from Trump’s $10bn defamation suit over the editing of a documentary in 2024. The earlier discovery order granted the broadcaster’s lawyers access to the financial information because, as the British legal writer David Allen Green explains, Trump had claimed that the editing of his speech to supporters on 6 January 2021, before they stormed the Capitol, had caused him massive reputational harm that cost his businesses vast sums of money. Framing the case that way let the BBC argue that it had a right to discovery on the actual state of Trump’s businesses. As Courthouse News reports, Trump’s lawyers now want to narrow the scope of his defamation claim against the broadcaster to prevent the full disclosure of his financial affairs. Life for Trump’s lawyers has not been made any easier by the fact that the president has, on at least five occasions since December, falsely claimed that the BBC did not just misleadingly edit his remarks from that day, but “used AI” to put words in his mouth that he did not say. The actual BBC edit at issue spliced together two parts of Trump’s remarks that were actually spoken 54 minutes apart, but made no use of AI and the words were spoken by him, and were not, as he has claimed again and again, “AI generated”. Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic nomination for the US Senate seat in Michigan, beating Haley Stevens in a bitter competition that became a referendum on the changing face of the Democratic party. El-Sayed won the race by a single point, fewer than 15,000 votes, according to the Associated Press. He will now face Republican nominee Mike Rogers – who ran unopposed – for a key battleground seat that is vital for Democrats to retain in order to achieve their lofty goal of reclaiming the majority in the upper chamber of Congress. More here Democrats quickly coalesced around El-Sayed following his narrow victory, urging their fractured coalition to back him with the goal of keeping the seat blue. Stevens said she has offered her “full support” to El-Sayed, while the Michigan senator Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat, said there is “nothing more important” than “uniting” and moving forward. More here Meanwhile, Republicans wasted no time painting El-Sayed as a vote for “complete insanity”. Rogers, the GOP nominee, said the Senate race was now about “whether Michigan has a future built on common sense – or whether we hand the keys to the most fringe extremists in the nation”. Donald Trump, for his part, said El-Sayed’s win was “great news” for Republicans, calling him a “communist loser”. Further down ballot, progressive Donavan McKinney beat incumbent Shri Thanedar in a closely watched Democratic primary for Michigan’s 13th congressional district. It was a contest that mirrored many of identity battles facing the party this midterm cycle. By a vote of 51-44, mainly along party lines, the Senate confirmed Erica Schwartz to lead the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), after the agency has gone without a permanent director for almost a year. The previous Senate-confirmed leader – Susan Monarez – was ousted by Robert F Kennedy Jr last August, after they clashed over the health secretary’s vaccine policy. It’s worth noting that Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan was the latest win for progressives across the country, many of whom challenged establishment-backed Democrats in key races across the country. Last month, Democratic socialist Melat Kiros unseated the long-serving US representative Diana DeGette in Colorado’s primary elections. And in New York, Brad Lander, Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, who were all backed by mayor Zohran Mamdani, also won races in the June congressional primaries. Lander won his race comfortably, defeating the two-term Democratic representative Dan Goldman. Valdez won against Antonio Reynoso – the handpicked successor of Nydia Velázquez. And Chevalier toppled Representative Adriano Espaillat, the powerful five-term incumbent who chairs the congressional Hispanic caucus. Despite progressive nominee Cori Bush’s loss in Missouri against pro-Israel incumbent Wesley Bell on Tuesday, Michigan insurgents in two key House races also claimed wins. A reminder that my colleagues are covering the latest developments out of the Middle East at our dedicated live blog. This includes the latest news that Iran and Oman have agreed a route for ships transiting the strait of Hormuz and are finalising the draft deal for jointly managing the vital chokepoint. However, Iran’s foreign ministry said that that any reopening of the strait would depend on the US fulfilling what Tehran sees as its commitment to end its own naval blockade of Iran’s ports. By a vote of 51-44, mainly along party lines, the Senate confirmed Erica Schwartz to lead the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), after the agency has been without a permanent director for almost a year. Tim Kaine of Virginia was the only Democrat to join all Republicans and vote yes on Schwartz’s nomination. Bernie Sanders, the independent senator from Vermont, congratulated the progressive Democrats he endorsed, who won in Michigan’s closely watched primary elections –including the Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. “Congratulations to Will Lawrence, Donavan McKinney and Dr Abdul El-Sayed on their historic victories last night,” Sanders said. title: Man arrested at Trump’s California golf course faces more charges
summary: Jeanine John Taele detained for ‘suspicious’ behavior and charged with possession of unregistered short-barreled rifle
body: A California man who was arrested at Donald Trump’s Los Angeles-area golf course ahead of a presidential visit is facing more charges, as authorities released more details about the investigation. Authorities say federal agents first observed 38-year-old Jeanine John Taele near the golf grounds in Rancho Palos Verdes on 31 July, wearing an earpiece and capturing photographs and videos of security agents assessing the property. Taele returned on 2 August, authorities say, two days before Trump was scheduled to visit the resort for a fundraising dinner with the Republican National Committee (RNC). Teale approached federal agents and said he was employed by the state department and was there for a security detail. After detaining Taele for “suspicious” behavior, Los Angeles county sheriff’s deputies found a loaded magazine in his pocket. In his pickup truck, which was parked at the golf club, deputies found a loaded 9mm pistol, binoculars and a badge labeled “security protection agent”, authorities have said. Law enforcement officers also recovered a trove of weapons from his residence in the nearby city of Downey, including a .45-caliber pistol, body armor, an illegally modified AR-type pistol, among others, officials said. Law enforcement officials also located notebooks containing “concerning statements” in the home. The Los Angeles county sheriff’s office declined to comment on the nature of the remarks. Taele was due in court Wednesday on a federal weapons charge but the hearing was cancelled. He was charged federally with possession of an unregistered short-barreled rifle that was found at this home, authorities said. The complaint alleges the firearm is an illegally modified AR-style rifle with a barrel that was cut down to 10in (25cm) from 14in (35cm). He is being held at a downtown LA jail on state charges, according to booking records. He was not yet in federal custody, said a spokesperson for the US attorney’s office. Taele is facing a misdemeanor charge for carrying a concealed weapon in a vehicle and two felony charges for possession of a short-barreled rifle or shotgun and the manufacture, importation or sale of a large-capacity magazine, court records show. The Los Angeles county public defender’s office, which is representing Taele in the state criminal case, declined to comment. Trump addressed the arrest on Tuesday, telling Fox News “only consequential presidents” are targeted, “and I am definitely consequential”, which he said brought him “a little solace”. Taele already appeared in court on state weapons charges and a second-degree robbery charge for an unrelated incident. “There is no room for error, particularly in light of previous attempts on President Trump’s life,” said Patrick Grandy, the assistant director in charge of the FBI’s Los Angeles office, in a statement. In April, Cole Tomas Allen, a California man who authorities say harbored resentment for the Trump administration, rushed past a security checkpoint during the White House correspondents’s association dinner, where the president was in attendance, and shot a firearm before being apprehended by Secret Service agents. He has been charged with an attempt to assassinate a US president, to which he has pleaded not guilty. In July 2024, a gunman opened fire at a rally where Trump spoke as the Republican presidential nominee. A crowd member was killed and a bullet grazed Trump’s ear. Federal agents fatally shot the suspected shooter, 20-year-old Thomas Matthew Crooks. An FBI investigation found no clear motive behind the deadly shooting. Ryan Routh was recently sentenced to life in prison after being convicted of attempting to assassinate Trump on a Florida golf course in September 2024. Prosecutors said Routh spent weeks plotting to kill Trump before aiming a rifle through shrubbery as Trump played golf at his West Palm Beach country club. Taele was a corporal in the US marines who was deployed to Iraq in 2008 and Afghanistan in 2010 and worked as a warehouse clerk, according to the US Marine Corps. He earned numerous commendations, including an award for good conduct, during his service from 2008 to 2016.

title: Toronto Zoo announces birth of pygmy hippo calf, third for mother Kindia
summary: The 20-year-old’s third calf is being monitored by officials as survival rates for the species are challenging, the zoo said
body: The Toronto Zoo has announced the birth of a female pygmy hippo calf. Kindia, the zoo’s 20-year-old pygmy hippo, started showing signs of labor at around 8.15am last Sunday, it said. Around four hours later, the calf’s feet emerged and after 1.5 hours of active labor, Kindia successfully gave birth to the baby pygmy hippo. Within 15 minutes of birth, the calf began trying to stand and was “confidently navigating the space” a few hours later, the zoo said, adding that the calf was seen nursing approximately 4.5 hours after birth. The zoo has not identified the calf yet, but said that it is doing well alongside its mother. According to the zoo, the newborn is Kindia’s third calf. Kindia became pregnant after she was introduced to a 31-year-old male pygmy hippo named Harvey for eight days in January. “This wonderful news comes with both hope and caution,” the zoo said. “Kindia successfully raised her daughter Penelope in 2018, and calf survival for this species can be challenging. Our team will continue to closely monitor both mom and calf around the clock during these important first days to ensure they continue to progress well together.” Noting the species’ endangered status on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list, Dolf DeJong, the Toronto Zoo’s CEO, said: “Welcoming a pygmy hippo calf is far more than a celebration of new life. Pygmy hippos are endangered, and their wild populations continue to decline due to habitat loss and human pressures. “This birth represents the critical role modern accredited zoos play in conservation, scientific collaboration, and maintaining healthy populations that contribute to the long-term survival of the species.” Only approximately 2,000 to 3,000 pygmy hippos are believed to remain in the wild. With adult pygmy hippos weighing anywhere from 330lb to 660lb and standing around 2.5 tall, the species are native to the forests and swamps of west Africa. In recent decades however, pygmy hippos have faced growing threats to their habitat including logging, mining, farming activities as well as human settlement.

title: White House confirms new helipad for supersized Marine One helicopter
summary: Changes come after report says Trump unhappy with helipad’s appearance and lawn’s slope
body: The White House has confirmed that contractors are redoing a new helipad built on the South Lawn to accommodate a new supersized Marine One chopper recently added to the presidential transport fleet. A White House official said the changes to the circular concrete landing pad were ordered as “we continue to make improvements as part of the ongoing project to best match the needs of the White House”. The Washington Post reported on Tuesday that Donald Trump was unhappy with the pad’s appearance and the lawn’s slope. The paper said construction crews had been working “around the clock” to finish the project, which the president hoped would be completed before the Chinese president Xi Jinping’s visit to the US in late September. While helicopters do not strictly require a level surface, the outlet said that downward gradient of the White House lawn, which slopes as much as 20 degrees in some spots, might also have to be changed so the helipad, too, could sit level with the horizon. Last week, a 100ft-wide granite presidential seal that was beginning to take shape was then observed to have been dug up again, the outlet observed. The helipad is the latest in Trump’s controversial improvement projects, including the construction of a White House ballroom on the side of East Wing and a new lining in the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool. Others on the drawing board include a garden of heroes and a triumphal arch complete with a 60ft gilded bronze winged Lady Liberty statue, flanked by a pair of enormous gilded eagles. The new helipad is expected to feature a carved granite presidential seal and cost $5m to $6m, funded entirely by helicopter manufacturer Sikorsky Aircraft. The new Marine One, a militarized variant of the Sikorsky S-92, or VH-92A Patriot, manufactured by Sikorsky Aircraft, has exhaust vents that direct heat downward. It is considerably larger and more powerful than the previous Sikorsky SH-3 Sea King. Security upgrades on the already larger new helicopter meant more weight, requiring the twin jet engines to work harder to take off and land while the vents directing heat downwardmake singeing the lawn more likely. The new VH-92A helicopter has been developed as the new Marine One for more than a decade. In 2024, Joe Biden rode it from Chicago’s O’Hare international airport to Soldier Field. Around the same time, the Marine Corps took delivery of the last of the 21-helicopter fleet – plus two test versions – “in support of the executive lift mission” at a cost $4.95bn, or about $215m each. Currently, Trump is using the Ellipse – a park south of the White House – as a landing pad for Marine One. “For years, the White House has desperately needed a proper Helipad on White House grounds that will allow the president to land safely and also protect the beautiful South Lawn grass from the fierce exhaust fumes of the incredible Marine One,” the White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in a statement. He added that “thanks to President Trump, the White House has never looked better, and it will only continue to get better under his leadership”.

title: Trump team pushes to block court order giving BBC access to financial records
summary: President has sued the broadcaster for $10bn, claiming a documentary on 2021 Capitol attack led to financial harm
body: Donald Trump’s legal team is making an 11th-hour attempt to block a court order that would grant the BBC access to the president’s financial records, as part of his multibillion-dollar lawsuit against the British broadcaster. Trump claims that the BBC’s 2024 documentary on the January 6 attacks have damaged the president’s business interests. In July, a Miami-based judge ruled that the president would have to start handing over detailed financial records to the BBC by 6 August. The records would reveal details into the hundreds of businesses owned by the US president’s family trust. Trump’s attorneys asked the court on Wednesday to temporarily pause the enforcement of the court order, arguing the BBC had demanded a “shockingly broad amount of information based on clearly political motivations”. Trump’s lawyers also asked the court to amend their initial lawsuit to instead focus on the “reputation harm” that was caused by the documentary, which would keep necessary disclosures “proportional to the needs of the case”, the lawyers said. While it is unclear what Trump’s net worth is, recent financial disclosures showed that he had made more than $2.2bn during his first year back in office. The lawsuit against the BBC is one of Trump’s several recent attempts to wage legal battles against media outlets that publish critical coverage of him. On Wednesday, Trump’s attorneys tried to argue that a $10bn defamation suit brought against the Wall Street Journal should go to a trial after it reported on a “bawdy” letter the president reportedly included in a birthday book for the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein in 2003. Trump’s justice department also issued and then recalled subpoenas to New York Times journalists after the paper reported on security concerns with the Air Force One presidential jet. Trump’s initial lawsuit concerns a scene in the BBC documentary, entitled Trump, A Second Chance, that spliced lines from a speech the president made on 6 January 2021. The clip made it appear like Trump directly urged his supporters to attack the US Capitol. The BBC has apologized for the edit but argued the defamation claims have no merit. Trump recently claimed that the BBC “used AI” to insert words into his speech, which the network has categorically denied.

title: New Mexico sues justice department for ‘stonewalling’ Epstein investigation
summary: Filing by attorney general Raúl Torrez comes after DoJ appears to have ignored deadline for key Epstein ranch files
body: New Mexico filed a lawsuit against the US Department of Justice and the acting attorney general, Todd Blanche, on Wednesday for “stonewalling” its criminal investigation into the activities of the late financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein at a remote ranch in the state. Raúl Torrez, the New Mexico attorney general, had said he was mulling the possibility of legal action if the justice department did not share with him by 31 July information about the alleged historical abuse of girls and young women at Epstein’s Zorro ranch about 30 miles south of Santa Fe. Wednesday’s filing, seen by the Guardian, delivers on that threat after the justice department appeared to ignore last Friday’s deadline. The lawsuit, filed in the US district court for the district of Columbia, alleges that Blanche and his department had “stonewalled” the state investigation Torrez reopened in February after the 10,000-acre Zorro property was mentioned thousands of times in recent releases of the so-called Epstein files. The government was compelled to release what it knew about Epstein’s activities and crimes by a transparency act signed by Donald Trump in November, but Democrats and critics have accused Blanche of covering up many of the files. Torrez said he wanted to establish what had taken place at Zorro, which, unlike other properties prominent in Epstein’s sex-trafficking conspiracy in Palm Beach, New York, and his private Caribbean island, saw no confirmed federal search take place. Epstein died in jail in New York in August 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges. He bought the ranch in 1993 from the estate of Bruce King, the Democratic former New Mexico governor, and numerous photographs of men and young girls there taken in the years thereafter featured in the latest Epstein files release. Additionally, a succession of survivors had previously given testimony about sexual and physical abuse they were subjected to at the ranch by Epstein and others. Torrez’s complaint asks for a declaration that Blanche and the justice department acted illegally in refusing to hand over any evidence it had about events at Zorro. It wants the court to direct the department to comply with the Epstein transparency law and so-called Touhy regulations governing how federal agencies handle requests for official documents during litigation. It also seeks costs and “such other and further relief as the Court deems just and proper”. Torrez said in a 14 July letter to Blanche that he would “pursue all available legal remedies without further notice” if the 31 July deadline passed. The attorney general said he had made “repeated, documented, good-faith efforts to obtain the unredacted investigative records in the DoJ’s custody”. The US attorney’s office for the district of New Mexico, in a statement to the Guardian last week, said it had “substantively responded” to Torrez’s request on 30 June by emailing 31 documents. But Torrez said the papers were mostly old news clippings and heavily redacted pages of little use to state investigators. He said full transparency was needed to advance the criminal investigation initially opened by Hector Balderas, his predecessor as New Mexico attorney general, in February 2019, and later mothballed at the request of federal prosecutors at the southern district of New York, which led a previous Epstein investigation. Those same prosecutors told Torrez last month that they “will not cooperate” in the New Mexico investigation, he said in a social media post on 14 July. The Guardian has contacted the justice department for comment on Wednesday’s filing. Additional reporting by Victoria Bekiempis

title: Top Democrats set aside qualms and embrace progressive Abdul El-Sayed
summary: Democrats are ‘united by a common purpose,’ Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand say in joint statement
body: Leading Democrats quickly papered over whatever qualms they had about progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed after his win in the Michigan Senate primary was confirmed on Wednesday, instead welcoming the former public health official as their champion against the Republican nominee, Mike Rogers. The state is now key to Democrats’s hopes of retaking control of the chamber in November’s midterm elections. Winning in Michigan would put them on the path to snarling Donald Trump’s legislative agenda and blocking his judicial nominees for the final two years of his presidency, while defeat could undermine their prospects of gaining a majority in the chamber for years to come. Rogers lost a Senate race in Michigan two years ago by a slim margin to Democrat Elissa Slotkin. “Democrats are united by a common purpose: putting a check on Donald Trump by defeating his Republican enablers and taking back the Senate. We look forward to working with Abdul and Democrats across Michigan to win this seat in November,” the Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, and Kirsten Gillibrand, who chairs the Democratic Senate campaign arm, said in a joint statement. Schumer was among a long list of Democratic establishment figures who had rallied behind Stevens in the weeks before the vote, as polls showed her trailing El-Sayed. He ultimately prevailed but by a far slimmer margin than data indicated, winning by 48.5% to Stevens’s 47.5%. “There’s a lot of passion and energy in these primaries, and that’s a good thing. Democrats are ready to beat Republicans across the state,” said Governor Gretchen Whitmer, who had endorsed Stevens. “We’re all united by our shared goal of getting things done for the people in Michigan.” The easiest path for Democrats to win back the Senate – which Republicans control with 53 lawmakers to their 47 – requires holding on to their seats in Michigan and Georgia while ousting Republicans from blue state Maine as well as three other red states. Democratic leaders believe they have the right candidates to pull that off in North Carolina, Ohio and Alaska, but it will nonetheless be a tall order, given that all three states backed Trump in 2024, and the latter two by double-digit margins. Michigan’s Democratic senator Gary Peters, whose decision not to seek re-election had sparked the primary for his seat, backed Stevens as his replacement but quickly endorsed El-Sayed after his primary. “Both candidates ran strong campaigns focused on improving the lives of all Michiganders. But now it’s time to come together as a party and rally around our nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, to make sure Mike Rogers never sees the floor of the US Senate,” Peters said. In a statement released following her loss, Stevens congratulated El-Sayed but did not outright endorse him, instead indicating she was ready to campaign for him as well as Democrats vying to win swing districts in Michigan. “This was a thorough and rigorous campaign that brought out the full span of views within the Democratic party – and that is why we have primaries. I am proud to have put up my hand to serve, and prouder to continue to work together to make sure this Senate seat remains blue, that we flip the United States Senate and continue the work for Michigan,” Stevens said. Republicans meanwhile pounced on El-Sayed’s views to paint him as too far left for voters in Michigan, a state that backed Trump in 2016 and again in 2024. “The choice this November is simple: common sense or complete insanity,” Rogers said. The former congressman blamed Democrats – who have held both of Michigan’s Senate seats since 2001 – for job losses in manufacturing, while saying El-Sayed “doesn’t represent a vision for the future. He’s leading a movement grounded in ideological fanaticism.” The question of aid to Israel animated the primary, with Stevens arguing Democrats should continue backing the US’s top ally in the Middle East and El-Sayed calling for an end to military support in response to its actions in Gaza and the West Bank. The United Democracy Project, a Super Pac connected to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, spent more than $30m in the race to support Stevens and oppose El-Sayed, to no avail, and he now joins insurgents in Denver, New York City, New Jersey and Philadelphia in having wooed Democratic voters in part by vowing to stand up for Palestinian rights. “Abdul’s victory is a win for everyone who supports equality, justice, and a thriving future for all,” said the IfNotNow Movement, a Jewish organization opposed to Israel’s policy towards Palestinians. “We urge those who see Abdul’s support for Palestinian human rights and blocking weapons to Israel as a threat to our community to reconsider. It is incredibly dangerous to conflate Jewish safety with support for Aipac or Israel’s military.” Brian Romick, president of the Democratic Majority for Israel Pac, called El-Sayed’s victory an indicator that “there is clearly strong anti-establishment energy this cycle, but no one should count pro-Israel Democrats out”. “While El-Sayed’s razor-thin victory in Michigan is disappointing, it was hardly the sweeping triumph he predicted or a mandate for his views,” Romick said, noting that Stevens lost only narrowly.

title: Drone carrying explosives at German airport marks ‘new level of danger’, says interior minister
summary: Investigators treating incident as part of ‘professional hybrid threat scenario’, says Alexander Dobrindt
body: Germany’s interior minister has warned that the discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport marks “a new level of danger” for the country, as authorities examine whether the thwarted attack could have been planned by a foreign power. The discovery of a small drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport, a leading shipping and military hub, set off alarm and caused flight diversions on Wednesday morning. German police deployed a bomb disposal robot to defuse and destroy the explosive device. In public remarks on Wednesday evening, the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said the incident did not appear to be the work of amateurs, and that investigators were treating it as part of a “professional hybrid threat scenario”. “We are dealing here with a competition that may also include foreign powers – this will be part of the investigations – who quite obviously want to contribute to considerable uncertainty in Germany,” Dobrindt said. A DHL cargo plane that had been forced to abort its landing at the airport then collided with an unknown object in mid-air as it was climbing away from the airport. It later landed safely elsewhere. Dobrindt and other German officials did not explicitly mention Russia as a potential suspect in their remarks. But the airport’s status as a Nato and German military logistics hub, as well as the base for Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines in Europe, has directed suspicion toward Russia, which has previously been accused of carrying out sabotage attacks in Europe. Security experts said the incident could amount to a serious escalation in tensions with Russia if it was determined the Kremlin played a role. Investigators said “a drone carrying an unknown explosive device was spotted by an airport employee in the security area of the cargo operations zone near the south runway” of Leipzig airport, a facility classified as “critical infrastructure”. “A suspected second unidentified flying object collided with a cargo aircraft after it had taken off again following the previous closure of the runway. Minor damage was detected on the aircraft after it landed in Hanover,” the investigators said. A Nato official said: “We are aware of the incident, which the German authorities continue to investigate.” The drone, a quadcopter that was fitted with an explosive device, was found near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane, according to media reports. Some of the Ukrainian aircraft are emblazoned with patriotic slogans including “Be Brave Like Kherson” and “Be Brave Like Bucha”, the site of a civilian massacre early in the full-scale Russian invasion. The tabloid Bild speculated that the explosive could have been fabricated ⁠from fertiliser and petrol, while a team from the public broadcasters NDR and WDR, as well as the Süddeutsche newspaper, said the device had contained pentaerythritol tetranitrate, or PETN – a primary ingredient in semtex that belongs to the same chemical family as nitroglycerin. Ukraine’s ambassador to Germany, Oleksii Makeiev, blamed Moscow. “Who else could it be but Russia?” he told the commercial broadcaster Welt TV. Moscow has not commented so far. Konstantin von Notz, the opposition Green party’s spokesperson on intelligence oversight, called for an investigation to be conducted with the utmost urgency and also hinted at possible Russian involvement. “Should it transpire that a state is behind this action, this would constitute not merely terrorism but state terrorism directed against the federal republic of Germany and its citizens,” he told Der Spiegel. Marc Henrichmann, the CDU chair of the German parliament’s intelligence oversight committee, said the latest incident looked like “an attempt to target a company of importance for Ukraine”. If the details are confirmed, it “would represent a new level of escalation in these sorts of attacks”, he told the Rheinische Post newspaper. Several aircraft, including a passenger plane from Mallorca, were diverted because of the incident. Operations in the northern part of the airport resumed two hours later. The southern runway, where the drone was found, remained closed. Police deployed a bomb disposal robot to examine the object. Police and prosecutors said: “There is no danger to the lives or safety of passengers or airport staff. Passenger air traffic is unaffected.” Germany and other European countries have had a series of suspicious unauthorised drone overflights at airports, military facilities, ports and logistics companies. They have accused Russian agents of being behind some of the flights, which Moscow has denied. Germany is the biggest single national supplier of military aid to Ukraine and has accused Russia of orchestrating a campaign of sabotage, espionage and disinformation against it, which the Kremlin has denied. Last year, a Chinese national was convicted for passing on information about flight schedules and cargo movements at Leipzig/Halle airport to a man spying for Beijing. Separately, Die Zeit reported that Russian secret services were plotting an attack against Stefan Thumann, the head of German drone manufacturer Donaustahl. The report said German investigators were tipped off by a foreign intelligence service at the end of last year and arrested a Ukrainian man and a Romanian woman this spring. Thumann is said to be under police protection. In 2024, US intelligence services reportedly foiled a Russian plot to assassinate the chief executive of Germany’s leading arms manufacturer, an apparent attempt at retaliation over the company’s role in providing a large amount of armaments for Ukraine. The plan to murder Armin Papperger, the chief executive of Rheinmetall, was reportedly one of several Russian government schemes to kill defence industry executives in several countries in Europe that have been supporting Ukraine’s war effort. The plot against Papperger was believed to be the most advanced. Additional reporting by Jakub Krupa

title: Senate confirms Trump pick Erica Schwartz as new CDC director
summary: Schwartz, president’s third pick to lead top US public health agency, confirmed in 51-44 Senate vote
body: Dr Erica Schwartz was confirmed by the US Senate as director ‌of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), a rare win for the Trump administration after a string of failed attempts to fill senior health posts. Schwartz was confirmed by a ⁠51-44 vote that broke largely along party lines, with Tim Kaine of Virginia the sole Democrat to support her nomination. Donald Trump’s third pick to run the CDC, Schwartz is set to take the reins of the agency after a tumultuous period of leadership turnover, and amid public concern over an outbreak of cyclosporiasis and Robert F Kennedy Jr’s hesitancy towards vaccines. At her confirmation hearing last month, senators pressed Schwartz on whether she would stand firm against any attempts by the health secretary to erode the scientific consensus around vaccines. She replied that she “will never betray the science” but generally deflected questions about how she would manage the relationship with Kennedy. “We need a CDC director that will ⁠actually stand up to crazy, stupid things being said that undermine faith in immunization,” said Bill Cassidy, the committee’s Republican chair and a physician. Schwartz replied that Kennedy “will absolutely allow me to be CDC director”, and Cassidy later announced his support for her nomination. “There are challenges facing Americans’ health today. I will work with her to face those challenges and regain trust in the CDC,” Cassidy said after the Senate confirmed her. A navy veteran, Schwartz served as deputy surgeon general during Trump’s first term, after positions in the United States Public Health Service where she was detailed to the Coast Guard, eventually becoming the force’s chief medical officer. Trump’s first nominee to lead the CDC, David Weldon, a former Florida congressman, was withdrawn by the White House in March 2025 just before his confirmation hearing. Schwartz will be the first permanent CDC director since Susan Monarez, Trump’s second pick, who was fired by Kennedy last year after less than a month over a clash on vaccine policy.

title: Republican who withdrew last month beats Trump-backed rival in Michigan
summary: Thomas Smith, whose name remained on ballot, beats Republican rivals in primary contest for eighth district
body: Thomas Smith withdrew from the Republican primary contest for Michigan’s eighth district last month. On Tuesday, he won the nomination. Unofficial results show Smith with more than 50% of the vote, according to the Associated Press, defeating the man he endorsed, anti-abortion activist Al Lemmo, and the man Donald Trump endorsed, former federal law enforcement officer Amir Hassan. In a statement on Wednesday, Smith said he was “humbled and honored that Republicans have chosen me to take the fight to Kristen McDonald Rivet”, the Democratic incumbent in the battleground House district. “I look forward to working with Speaker [Mike] Johnson and the entire Republican team to expand our House majority and advance President Trump’s ‘America first’ agenda to lower costs for working families and make America affordable again,” he added. In June, Trump endorsed Hassan, an African American navy veteran who worked for the Departments of Defense, Homeland Security and Transportation. The president also appeared with Hassan at a campaign event in Michigan. Hassan said during his campaign that he had recently converted to Christianity from Islam. Nonetheless, social media commentary suggests Republican voters did not view Hassan’s conversion as authentic and were apprehensive about nominating a Muslim candidate. “It was a tough race, but over the last year I’ve had some incredible dealings with people across the entire district,” Hassan said in a video posted to X and Facebook. “The biggest conservative value is that we don’t make excuses.” In a statement, Joe Gruters, the chair of the Republican National Committee, congratulated Smith on a “hard-fought, well-earned primary victory”. Smith, who did little campaigning, posted on social media in July to endorse Lemmo, describing Hassan as a crypto-Republican. In Michigan, a US House candidate must withdraw their candidacy before 24 April for election officials to have enough time to remove their name from ballots. The Federal Election Commission has no electronic campaign finance filings from Smith. It does have a handwritten letter dated 12 July declaring $1,850 in fundraising. “I could not file this electronically because I have had no success logging in and have not been able to get a response from the helpdesk,” Smith wrote in a postscript on the letter. The Flint native and retired General Motors engineer made a brief appearance at a Republican unity event hosted in Macomb county by Mike Rogers, the party’s newly minted Senate candidate. Smith said he intended to “unseat communist comrade Rivet”. Though the victory on Tuesday of Abdul El-Sayed in the Democratic Senate primary has drawn national attention to progressive politics in Michigan, Rivet has signaled her relative moderation as one of 10 House Democrats to join Promise to America, a congressional initiative led by US representatives Tom Suozzi of New York and Adam Gray of California explicitly embracing capitalism and rejecting socialism. The congressional district along Michigan’s Saginaw River, connecting Flint to the Saginaw Bay, was one of 13 districts nationwide that voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election while also electing a Democratic representative to Congress.

title: Adapting to global heating: which UK public services are struggling in hot weather?
summary: As NHS told to prepare for extreme weather, strain also felt in other areas including transport and farming
body: The NHS has been told it must become more resilient to increasingly frequent heatwaves supercharged by the climate crisis, as the UK government puts adaptation to extreme heat high on its agenda. But what other public services are already feeling the strain? Transport London bus drivers plan to go on strike later this month over their working conditions, as many have been experienced cab temperatures reaching close to 40C in the recent heat. Most London buses are fitted with air-flow cooling systems rather than air conditioning. Sadiq Khan, the mayor, has said drivers should not be working in unsafe hot conditions, but Arriva, the private operator, has said it will take time to update its fleet. Rail services have also been disrupted as the shrinkage of soil due to the dry weather has made embankments unsafe in the south of England because sleepers, part of the tracks, can move or drop out of position. Heat can also warp rails, leading operators to impose lower speed limits for safety. On the roads, the RAC has reported that breakdowns have soared by a fifth, often owing to engines overheating, or tyre blowouts on overheated road surfaces. Farming and food This year’s harvest could be the worst on record, analysis published on Wednesday found, as the third year running of drought in England left farmers with dry soil and damaged crops. Cereals and oilseed yields could be down as much as 2.5m tonnes across the UK, worth £390m in lost revenue for arable farmers, according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank. Livestock farmers are also under pressure: grass growth has halved, forcing some to use feed they had hoped to save for winter. This followed an unusually wet start to the year but most farms are not in a position to store water adequately on their farms. The Country Land and Business Association (CLA), representing landowners, is calling for planning reforms to make small reservoirs on farms easier, while some regenerative farming practices can also help to store more water on land. If dry conditions persist into autumn, farmers will have further problems preparing for next year. Tom Lancaster, the food and farming analyst at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) thinktank, said: “At the start of spring, farmers were hopeful of a better year, but the dry April and July and record-breaking heat have left farmers facing down the barrel of a third awful harvest in a row. “Farming is now the sector most exposed to climate change and the risks and damage that it brings. From the wettest winter on record in 2024, to the hottest summer in 2025 and now unprecedented heat and drought this year, we are in danger of UK farming entering a climate doom loop, as repeated impacts undermine the capacity of farmers to drill next year’s crop.” As farmers have struggled, the price of fresh food has risen. The wholesale price of tomatoes is up by more than 60%, iceberg lettuce by 90% and potatoes by more than 40%. The outlook abroad is gloomy too, with a super El Niño increasingly possible, so relying on imports to make up the shortfall may bring more problems with it. Working conditions The UK does not have a maximum legal temperature for workers, and employees have struggled, particularly those working in poorly repaired public buildings. Court cases have been disrupted, with one judge in Bristol telling a jury in July they had to listen to a defendant through a virtual link because the dock was unusable in the heat. Some public libraries that are already equipped with air conditioning are operating as “cool spaces” for communities. Maps can be found online showing where they are available. Paul Nowak, secretary general of the TUC, told the Guardian: “After a summer of heatwaves, it is clear we need to adapt to the climate crisis.” Employers need to keep staff working indoors and outdoors safe, with regular breaks or flexible working, proper equipment and access to water, he said, but legislation was also needed. “As heatwaves become our new normal, we need to find ways to work and live with hot weather,” he said. “That means new laws on maximum working temperatures, adapting buildings and workplaces to keep them cool, and ambitious climate action to tackle the problem at its root.” Schools Pupils are off at the moment, escaping the stuffy classrooms that reduced some to tears in the summer term, but some of the inequalities in the UK’s education system continue: the Guardian revealed that private schools were continuing to water their lawns, despite hosepipe bans covering close to half of England and some of Wales. The heat should be less severe when most return in September, but the Climate Change Committee has called for all schools to have air conditioning by 2050, and for a rethink of the traditional school year. It suggested that having exams in June may no longer be the most sensible way of arranging the academic timetable, given evidence that heat can affect pupils’ test performance.

title: Iran and Oman agree on coordinates of route through strait of Hormuz, says Iranian foreign ministry – as it happened
summary: Joint announcement for geographic coordinates being finalised, says spokesperson, adding that it would not guarantee security in waterway
body: Iran and Oman have agreed a route for ships transiting the strait of Hormuz and are finalising the draft deal for jointly managing the waterway, Tehran’s foreign ministry said Wednesday. But, spokesperson Esmaeil Baghei stressed that any reopening of the strait would depend on the United States fulfilling what Tehran sees as its commitment to end its own naval blockade of Iran’s ports. A joint statement will be issued from Iran and Oman “if certain parties do not obstruct this process” , Baghei said, apparently referring to the US. Two regional officials briefed on the negotiations told the AP that the potential deal was a temporary solution to the dispute over the strait, and will pave the way for the US and Iran to resume negotiations on Tehran’s nuclear program. Israel launched attacks in southern Lebanon after accusing Hezbollah of violating the ceasefire, despite ongoing US-mediated peace talks between Israel and Lebanon in Rome. At least one person was killed and 11 others injured in Israeli strikes on the southern town of Tibnin. The strikes came after the IDF issued a warning for people in the southern village of Mansouri to flee their homes – the first time in more than a month that the military had issued such an order ahead of an imminent strike. It comes as the United Nations said more than 800,000 people displaced by war have begun returning to their homes in Lebanon. Oil prices rose after Yemen’s ⁠Iran-aligned Houthi rebels said they targeted a Saudi oil tanker in the Red Sea as part of their naval blockade of Saudi Arabia. Brent crude futures were up 81 cents, or 1.02%, at $80.17 a barrel by 12pm GMT. ⁠US West Texas Intermediate futures gained 34 cents, or 0.45%, to $76.11. The Houthis said they had launched a missile attack on a Saudi ‌oil tanker off the coast ‌of Yanbu, a key port for Saudi crude oil exports. This is the eighth ship they have attacked since 22 July, when they announced that they were imposing a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia. Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian said in an interview aired by state TV on Wednesday that interaction with the country’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei is currently “very difficult”. Mojtaba has not made any public appearances since he became supreme leader, replacing his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in one of the first strikes launched against Iran by the US and Israel. More on the Houthi attacks. The group “successfully targeted the Saudi oil tanker Wafa in the northern Red Sea, off the coast of Yanbu, with a number of ballistic missiles,” spokesman Yahya Saree said in a video statement. In a later statement, Saree said the rebels targeted the “Saudi oil tanker Daisy in the Gulf of Aden with a ballistic missile”, referring to the waterway that connects to the Red Sea. The Houthis declared they will escalate attacks in the northern Red Sea because Saudi Arabia is diverting its oil tankers there from the south in response to their blockade. Nine Saudi oil tankers have been targeted since the start of the blockade last month, according to figures given by a Houthi military spokesman. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said they targeted a Saudi Arabian oil vessel in the Gulf of Aden, the group’s military spokesperson said in a statement, Reuters reported. The Houthis said they also launched a missile attack on a Saudi oil tanker off the coast of the kingdom’s Red Sea port city of Yanbu. There was no confirmation from Saudi Arabia on either incident. The Houthis’ military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, did not say when the attacks took place. On Tuesday, the Houthis warned shipping companies that their tankers risk being attacked if they use Saudi Arabian ports. The Houthis imposed a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea last month in response to what they described as a Saudi siege on Yemen, an allegation Riyadh has denied. US Central Command said its forces have redirected 48 commercial vessels, disabled two and boarded two as part of its Iran blockade. Vessels in the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on 3 August. According to the Associated Press, Iranian and Omani negotiators have finalised the draft deal to reopen the strait of Hormuz and are awaiting final approval from Iran’s supreme leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei. A reminder that Khamenei is believed to have been injured in the war’s opening strikes on 28 February and has not been seen in public since then. Two regional officials briefed on the negotiations portrayed the potential deal to the AP as a temporary solution to the dispute over the strait. They said it is tied to an agreement reached between the US and Iran in June that aimed at ending the fighting and reopening the waterway, but ultimately collapsed. The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the private talks, told the AP that the potential deal will pave the way for the US and Iran to resume negotiations on Tehran’s nuclear program. Earlier, they had said the possible agreement would have ships enter the Persian Gulf through an Iranian-controlled route and exit through a route controlled by Oman. Service fees would be charged for providing security and preserving the maritime environment, the officials said. The US has said it is strongly opposed to any arrangement that would see Iran charge fees. As we reported earlier, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, said that the agreement with Oman is in the “final stage” of drafting, and that a joint statement will be issued “if certain parties do not obstruct this process” - apparently referring to the United States. The UK’s Maritime Trade Operations centre (UKMTO) has said that a vessel off the coast of Yemen has reported a loud explosion nearby. The incident took place 95 nautical miles (176kms) southeast of Aden, UKMTO said in an update shared on X, adding that all the vessels’ crew are “accounted for and safe”. More on that now. According to Iranian state news agency IRNA, foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghei said: “The geographical coordinates of the route envisaged by the two sides have been agreed upon and, if certain third parties do not obstruct the process, the joint statement of the two countries, containing the main considerations and points of agreement, is also in the final review and drafting stage.” According to the report, Baghei told reporters that talks with Oman were moving forward, but that even if an understanding was reached, it would not mean that the strait had become safe for all passing vessels. “The factors making the Strait of Hormuz insecure still exist on the part of the United States, particularly the naval blockade and other aggressive and threatening actions against Iran and its interests,” he said. The ⁠geographic coordinates for a shipping ⁠route ⁠through the strait of Hormuz ⁠have been agreed by Iran and ⁠Oman, and a ‌joint announcement ‌is being ‌finalised, provided no third parties interfere, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei ‌said on Wednesday. Baghaei added that any such agreement between Iran and ⁠Oman would not, by itself, guarantee security in the strategic waterway. As we reported earlier, oil prices ⁠rose on Wednesday after Yemen’s ⁠Iran-aligned Houthi rebels said they attacked a Saudi oil tanker in the Red Sea, denting hopes of a de-escalation in Iran war hostilities that ⁠could restore shipping traffic and oil flows in the region. Brent crude futures were up 81 cents, or 1.02%, at $80.17 a barrel by 12pm GMT. ⁠US West Texas Intermediate futures gained 34 cents, or 0.45%, to $76.11. The Houthis said they had launched a missile attack on a Saudi ‌oil tanker off the coast ‌of Yanbu, a key port for Saudi crude oil exports. This is the eighth ship they have attacked since 22 July, when they announced that they were imposing a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia. There is a “50-50” chance that Iran and Oman will reach a deal to reopen the strait of Hormuz on Friday, a senior Gulf official familiar with the talks has told CNN, despite Donald Trump suggesting an agreement could come as early as Wednesday. As we reported earlier, Iran has said its talks with Oman to reopen the strait of Hormuz were progressing “positively”. The Gulf source told CNN that the Iranian delegation does not include the voice of the hardline Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which would have to sign off on the details of a provisional agreement. Meanwhile, Donald Trump has claimed a deal could be reached on Wednesday, with continued diplomatic efforts potentially paving the way for US-Iran talks to resume. “It could happen. Tomorrow or the next day,” the US president told reporters on Tuesday night. “A lot of progress has been made.” It followed similar statements from his secretary of state Marco Rubio and treasury secretary Scott Bessent, both of whom said progress had been made in those talks. Tehran, however, has denied that it is speaking with Washington and instead focused solely on its negotiations with Oman. Lebanon’s official National News Agency (NNA) has reported that one person was killed and 11 others injured in Israeli strikes on the southern town of Tibnin. The report came moments after the IDF announced it had begun strikes in southern Lebanon. Earlier, the Israeli military had also issued a forced evacuation order for people to flee the southern village of Mansouri. Here are some of the latest images from Lebanon on the newswires: The IDF has issued a brief update saying it has begun “targeted strikes” in southern Lebanon, which it said were in response to Hezbollah breaching the ceasefire. It came shortly after the IDF ordered people to flee the village of Mansouri (see previous post). We will bring you more as we get it. The Israeli military has issued a warning for people in the southern Lebanese village of Mansouri to flee their homes. It is the first time in more than a month that the military has issued such an order ahead of an imminent strike. The Israe…

title: US to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuum
summary: State department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and Cameroon
body: The US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and the Caribbean, drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of being filled by China. The US Congress has been served notice of the impending closures, which are being justified on cost grounds and follow a reassessment of the US’s bilateral relationships with a range of countries since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025. According to a notice served to several congressional committees, missions will close in St George’s, Grenada; Nagoya, Japan; Medan, Indonesia; Douala, Cameroon; and Winnipeg, Canada. The closures will continue a process of cutbacks in US state department operations overseen by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. Last year, the department fired more than 1,300 employees, including 246 foreign services officers and 1,107 civil servants. More than half of the US’s 195 ambassadorial posts around the world remain unfilled, including in keys locations such as Germany, Cuba, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, according to the American Foreign Service Association. Democrats have criticized the latest planned closures, saying it risked leaving the field free for China. “China has a diplomatic presence in three of the five locations where the state department is closing shop and Beijing is going to exploit that new vacuum to undercut American interests,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee. “The yearly operating costs of these diplomatic facilities represent a tiny fraction of the state department’s yearly budget,” Shaheen added. “Is that worth pulling back from these places where China is present?” The decision to close the consulate in Winnipeg has come in for criticism in Canada, on which Trump recently announced the imposition of 50% tariffs on a range of goods. Opened in 2001, the Winnipeg consulate has served to facilitate trade and investment issues mainly relating to the province of Manitoba, of which Winnipeg is the capital. Brad Kirbyson, a former political specialist who worked at the consulate for 20 years, told the Canadian broadcaster CBC the closure could harm US interests. “I’m sure it’ll save them a few dollars, but I think the net effect is to lose touch with a broad swath of Canada by not having a presence there,” he said. “The United States found that it was a very long way between the US consulate in Calgary and the [one] in Toronto. “It makes a lot of sense to have a consulate in the middle of the country that can cover issues in this part of the world.” A spokesperson for the Canadian embassy in Washington said: “Canada and the US have a long history of collaboration on areas of shared interest, including through our foreign offices in both countries.” China does not have a diplomatic mission in Winnipeg, but it has a presence in St George’s, Nagoya and Medan. The US mission in St George’s, the capital of the Caribbean island of Grenada, has full embassy status, while the Douala facility is defined as an “embassy branch office”. A state department spokesperson said: “The department is committed to following congressional notification procedures including post closures. We have nothing further to report at this time. “We are focused on ensuring our diplomatic footprint is efficient, effective and delivers results for the American people.” The White House’s office of management and budget has argued for a much more extensive closure program of up to 30 foreign missions. Democrats, supported by national security and foreign policy specialists, have countered that such moves will dangerously reduce the US’s diplomatic footprint and global influence, especially when combined with last year’s dismantling of USAID, the main overseas development body, which was drastically reduced in size before being bundled into the state department.

title: New York City transit auctions off last MetroCard machines: ‘Wild home decor idea’
summary: MTA to sell remaining machines – which weigh up to 1,050lbs – as it transitions to contactless fare system
body: The Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) of New York City has begun auctioning off its final MetroCard vending machines, offering New Yorkers the chance to own one of the transit system’s most recognizable fixtures as the agency continues its transition to Omny. The auction opened on Wednesday morning and will run through 19 August, according to the MTA. The agency is offering a limited number of retired MetroCard Vending Machines (MVM) and MetroCard Express Machines (MEM), which have served subway riders for decades. “First installed in 1999, the colorful metal MVM and MEM are familiar to the millions of riders who take the subway each day,” the MTA said in a news release. The MTA’s media liaison, Joana Flores, confirmed the agency was auctioning off the very last of the machines. “Today, we began auctioning off the last MetroCard vending machines. There are a total of 60,” Flores said. The last remaining public-facing machine is located in Greenwich Village’s Mulry Square, she said, and now displays a QR code for commuters to scan should they be interested in making a bid. The larger MetroCard vending machines, first installed in 1999, allowed riders to buy and reload MetroCards using cash, credit and debit cards. Each machine measures 80in long, 42in wide and 36in deep (203cm x 107cm x 91cm), and weighs 1,050lbs (476kg). The smaller MetroCard express machines, introduced later to ease congestion at busy stations by accepting only credit and debit card payments, measure 21in long, 14in wide and 42in, and weigh about 210lb. The MTA said the machines were being sold as-is in non-operational condition after their electronic and payment processing components were removed. Successful bidders will be required to pay in full on the day they are notified and arrange pickup within 10 days. Buyers are responsible for loading and transporting the heavy machines. Flores said the MTA was also holding a public sweepstake in conjunction with the auction. Fifteen people will be selected in a random draw that allows the winners to skip the line at the agency’s annual transit memorabilia pop-up sale in October, along with a 20% discount on purchases. She added that any remaining vending machines not sold through the auction will be sold online through GovDeals. But the agency does not anticipate any will be left by then, Flores said: “Usually, these things are hot-ticket items – they tend to go fast.” The MetroCard, once synonymous with being a New York subway commuter, was also a popular vehicle for promotions, with the city issuing several commemorative editions, including one to mark baseball’s home-team World Series between the Mets and the Yankees in 2000. Many famous musicians graced the card over the years, such as David Bowie, Olivia Rodrigo, the Wu-Tang Clan, the Notorious BIG and LL Cool J, as did New York-centric TV shows such as Seinfeld and Law & Order. Some social media users have already expressed interest in placing bids, with commenters responding “Wild home decor idea” and “So tempted by this”. The NPR gameshow host Peter Sagal wrote: “I haven’t been a New Yorker since 1998 but I really, really want one.” The auction comes as the MTA continues replacing MetroCards with Omny, its contactless fare payment system. “We’re no longer selling MetroCards, but we are accepting MetroCards,” Flores said. There is no date yet for when the transit system plans to fully convert to contactless payments and stop accepting the classic yellow cards, but Flores said there will come a day when the agency will “transition fully over to the tap and ride system”.

title: Exiled PM vows to return to Bangladesh despite execution threat
summary: Sheikh Hasina plans a December comeback two years after being ousted in a bloody uprising led by students
body: Bangladesh’s ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina has vowed to return home by the end of the year, even though she faces a death sentence. “They may put me in a cell. They may kill me. Anything may happen, but still I have to go,” said Hasina, two years after a student-led uprising toppled her government. Hasina, 78, who has lived under tight security in India since fleeing Dhaka, said on Wednesday she would return in December – Bangladesh’s “month of victory”, marking the defeat of Pakistani forces in the 1971 war of independence. “Whatever fate awaits me, I will return to my people,” the former Awami League leader told a news conference at the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia in Delhi, speaking via audio link. Her son, Sajeeb Wazed Joy, told the news conference she was being treated well in exile. “She is staying with the full services and security of a head of state,” he said. “Prime minister [Narendra] Modi’s government has shown her the utmost respect, and for that I am eternally grateful.” India officially distanced itself from the news conference, saying it had no role in organising it and did not endorse the political views expressed. India has been walking a diplomatic tightrope over Hasina, who was one of its closest regional allies. Bilateral ties have deteriorated sharply since her downfall and India has been seeking to mend relations with Bangladesh while resisting demands for her extradition. Hasina’s flight ended more than 15 years of increasingly authoritarian Awami League rule. The Bangladesh Nationalist party, led by Tarique Rahman, the son of the former prime minister Khaleda Zia, swept to power earlier this year in an election that barred the Awami League. The government has said Hasina would probably be arrested the moment she set foot in Bangladesh. Last November, Bangladesh’s international crimes tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over the violent suppression of the protests. The demonstrations began over government-job quotas and snowballed into a mass movement against Hasina’s government. The UN estimates up to 1,400 people may have died. Hasina’s supporters say the death toll was about 800. She has rejected the court’s verdict as politically motivated and said the execution threat would not change her plans. Hasina was imprisoned several times during her fierce rivalry with Zia, who died in 2025. The two women traded claims of using corruption cases and arrests against each other in a “Battle of the Begums”, an honorific title for a senior woman. Bangladesh has prohibited domestic media from broadcasting or publishing Hasina’s statements. She has demanded that the ban on the Awami League be lifted, political prisoners be released and “false cases” against party activists be dropped. Claiming Bangladesh is sinking into lawlessness and economic ruin, she accuses the new government of trying to erase the country’s secular character. The government has been grappling with high inflation and sluggish economic growth while blaming many of the country’s problems on alleged corruption and mismanagement during Hasina’s years in power.
